# Additive smooths

A smooth function of one covariate was enough to let kyphosis rise and fall with age. This chapter puts more than one covariate into that smooth.

## Sums of smooth functions

A completely free surface $g(x_1,x_2,x_3)$ can be fitted, and in four covariates it cannot even be pictured. We do not use it. The model that stays readable replaces the linear predictor by a sum of univariate smooths, one per covariate. On the logit scale for kyphosis,
$$
\mathrm{logit}\,\mathrm{P}(\text{kyphosis})
=\beta_0+g_1(\text{number})+g_2(\text{start})+g_3(\text{age}).
$$
Each $g_j$ has its own penalty. Nothing forces them to be equally smooth. This is a generalised additive model, in the sense of Hastie and Tibshirani: additive in the smooths, not linear in the covariates. `Number` takes only the values $1$ through $8$, and `Start` only sixteen vertebral positions, so a smooth cannot have more knots than there are distinct values.
```r
need <- function(pkg) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(pkg, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
  }
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(pkg, character.only = TRUE))
}
need("mgcv")
need("rpart")
data(kyphosis, package = "rpart")
kyphosis$Kyphosis <- as.numeric(kyphosis$Kyphosis == "present")
summary(gam(Kyphosis ~ s(Number, k = 8) + s(Start, k = 16) + s(Age),
            family = binomial, data = kyphosis))
```
The equivalent degrees of freedom are about $1.19$ for the number of vertebrae, $2.04$ for the starting position, and $2.21$ for age.

![The three smooths in the additive kyphosis model, on the log-odds scale and centred at zero. Number of vertebrae is close to a straight line. Starting position is flat through the upper vertebrae and then falls. Age still rises and then eases.](../figures/kyphosis-additive.pdf){#fig-kyph-add}

In @fig-kyph-add, number is almost a straight line on the log-odds scale: more vertebrae in the same operation, higher odds of kyphosis. Start is flat from the top of the spine through about the sixth vertebra and then falls. Surgery that begins low on the back has the smaller risk. Age, now conditional on the other two, still rises and then eases, a little less dramatically than when it was the only covariate.

Each curve is the effect of moving that one covariate while the others are held fixed. Holding the starting vertebra at $16$ and imagining ten vertebrae below it is not a spine that exists. The sentence is conditional on a hypothetical, and some of those hypotheticals are empty.

A free function of all three covariates together would fit a surface we could not explain to a surgeon. Two-way interactions are already hard. Three-way interactions are where we stop. The compromise is a partially linear model: a coefficient for the term you want a unit-change sentence about, and a smooth for the terms you are only adjusting for. Ambient temperature in a lab, or the weight of a patient in a trial of two treatments, is the second kind. Dose and treatment are the first kind.

Number of vertebrae looked linear, so force it to be a slope and leave start and age smooth:
```r
need <- function(pkg) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(pkg, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
  }
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(pkg, character.only = TRUE))
}
need("mgcv")
need("rpart")
data(kyphosis, package = "rpart")
kyphosis$Kyphosis <- as.numeric(kyphosis$Kyphosis == "present")
summary(gam(Kyphosis ~ Number + s(Start, k = 16) + s(Age),
            family = binomial, data = kyphosis))
```
The slope on number is $0.333$ with standard error $0.232$ ($z=1.43$, $p=0.15$). Once start and age are in the model, the number of vertebrae is not detected. We would drop it. Start remains, with equivalent degrees of freedom about $2.03$. One printout gave $p=0.013$ for start and $p=0.071$ for age; `mgcv` 1.8 prints about $0.015$ and $0.078$. Age stays borderline either way, and we keep it for the same reason as in the previous chapter. The important covariate is where the operation starts. On the plotted smooth, the log-odds for a start among vertebrae $1$ to $5$ sit several units above the log-odds for a start at the bottom of the spine. That gap can be read as a factor of about $\exp(5)=148$ on the odds scale. A gap of $4$, which is also a fair reading of the same curve, is $\exp(4)\approx 55$. We will not pretend the graph yields one integer. The comparison is large, it favours starting lower, and it is conditional on age.

::: {.callout-note}
## Key idea
Smooth the covariates you are adjusting for and do not need a one-sentence answer about. Keep a parametric term for the covariate whose unit change you intend to report. A smooth of everything is a picture, not an effect.
:::

## Exercises

1. In the additive kyphosis model, `Number` has equivalent degrees of freedom $1.19$. Say what that number claims about the shape on the log-odds scale, and why `k = 8` is a ceiling rather than a target.
